newsitem.title: USA: Sprint takes Internet product to NFL fans.
newsitem.headline: Sprint takes Internet product to NFL fans.

text.p: Sprint Corp. this week will kick off its effort to score a touchdown with America's most dedicated football fans and win their Internet accounts.

The long-distance phone company has teamed up with the National Football League to develop a football-centric version of its Sprint Internet Passport product. It is the latest step in the Kansas City, Mo.-based company's continuing niche approach to gaining market share in Internet access service.

While it has been the perhaps largest player among the phone companies on the wholesale side of the Internet business -- providing background network services to such Internet providers as America Online Inc. -- Sprint has kept a conspicuously low profile when it comes to developing a retail customer base.

Internet analysts estimate that Sprint, with about 110,000 on-line users, has just one-tenth of the customer base of AT&T Corp. and about one-sixth of the subscribers of MCI Communications Corp.. It's not even in the same league as AOL, which has some 8.5 million subscribers.
"They've been perhaps the quietest of the telcos," said Ted Julian, an Internet analyst with International Data Corp in Framingham, Mass. "Sprint's strategy hasn't been as apparent as the others."

Company officials say their low, or slow, profile is deliberate. Sprint has purposely shunned a mass-marketing approach, they said. It has chosen instead to seek a controlled customer base through focused marketing campaigns targeted at groups with specific interests in common.
"We take an interest that people have off-line and show them how easy it is to pursue it online," Sprint spokesman Jeff Shafer said.
"We want to deliver to people who want it a relevant Internet experience," said Jeff Hallock, who led the team responsible for developing the NFL package.

Previous marketing efforts, for instance, include a campaign coordinated with Viacom Inc.'s Blockbuster video rental unit targeted at movie lovers, and a much smaller campaign for doctors belonging to the California Medical Association.

In the new campaign, Sprint, which already has a close relationship with the NFL, will mail thousands of versions of its access software to NFL season ticket subscribers. It is hoping to tap into the NFL's reputation for having a dedicated fan base that is also considered highly computer-literate.
The product will offer subscribers the standard full access to the Internet, with a choice between a $19.95 monthly flat rate for unlimited use or a $1.50 per hour rate.

But it will be geared specifically to users' presumed interest in football by providing a home, or start-up, page that offers a variety of direct links to football Internet sites, such as NFL.com, team clubhouses, ABC's Monday Night Football and online football merchandise catalogs.
"It will be really, really football-centric," Hallock said.
